[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing remote early-career employees with structured synchronous mentorship versus asynchronous-only mentorship, measuring explicit knowledge transfer via pre/post-tests and project performance metrics — Directly tests the causal claim by manipulating the presence of scheduled synchronous check-ins and measuring explicit knowledge transfer outcomes, addressing the disputed status with controlled evidence.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on remote mentorship programs (post-2020) focusing on the role of synchronous communication frequency and structure in knowledge transfer outcomes — Synthesizes existing empirical findings to assess the overall effect size and moderators (e.g., industry, team size), providing a broader evidence base to confirm or refute the hypothesis beyond single studies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of media richness and social presence applied to remote mentorship, predicting that scheduled synchronous check-ins enhance explicit knowledge transfer by reducing ambiguity and increasing engagement in distributed settings — Provides a mechanistic explanation that can be tested against empirical data; if predictions align with observed outcomes, it supports the hypothesis; if not, it suggests boundary conditions or refutation.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study comparing knowledge retention and task performance of early-career remote employees participating in structured mentorship programs versus those relying on informal peer networks, within global tech companies. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring tacit knowledge preservation outcomes (e.g., error rates, problem-solving speed) over the first year of employment, controlling for organizational culture and team size.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on remote onboarding practices, focusing on tacit knowledge transfer mechanisms (e.g., documented processes, virtual shadowing, structured check-ins) versus organic peer interactions. — Synthesizes prior findings to assess whether structured programs consistently outperform informal networks in preserving tacit knowledge, while identifying moderators like task complexity or communication tool quality.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework drawing on Nonaka and Takeuchi's SECI model, adapted for remote work, to predict how structured scaffolding (e.g., explicit articulation, simulation) may better externalize and internalize tacit knowledge than ad-hoc peer exchanges. — Provides a causal mechanism explaining why structured programs might be more effective, enabling generation of testable predictions about specific conditions (e.g., high turnover, low social presence) where the effect holds or reverses.
